newsitem.title: INDIA: Chinese demand seen spurring India soymeal exports.
newsitem.headline: Chinese demand seen spurring India soymeal exports.

text.p: Surging demand from China and low domestic consumption will keep Indian soymeal exports in 1996/97 at last year's levels despite a lower crop forecast, exporters said on Wednesday.
"We expect exports to be of the same level in the current season as last year," Satyanarayan Saboo, a leading soymeal exporter, told Reuters.
"Soymeal export prospects are good due to promising demand from China and Southeast Asian countries," said Navinbhai Shah, president of Bombay Oilseeds and Oil Exchange Ltd.

India exported 2.4 million tonnes of soymeal in 1995/96 (November-October). It exported 300,000 tonnes to China that year and those exports in would be substantially higher in 1996/97, exporters said.
"The demand from China has increased because of their lower soybean crop forecast in the current crop season," said one analyst, who asked not to be identified.
Traders said Indian soymeal was also in good demand from Indonesia, Malaysia, South Korea and the Philippines.
Soybean was currently quoted between 12,200 ($340) and 12,500 rupees per tonne in the local markets compared with 10,000-10,400 in the same period a year earlier.
"Local demand has gone down because prices are high. Therefore more is available for exports," Saboo said.
The Central Organisation of Oil Industry and Trade (COOIT) earlier this month estimated the 1996/97 soybean crop at 4.06 million tonnes, down from 4.45 million in the previous season.
Unfavourable weather in October in the central Indian state of Madhya Pradesh contributed to the fall in output.
Madhya Pradesh accounts for nearly 80 percent of the country's soybean production.
Competition for Indian soymeal was firming as the harvest of the Brazilian soymeal crop, which has a protein content of 48 percent, equal to that of Indian soymeal, starts in a few days.

"Now the Brazilian harvest will start and it will compete with Indian soymeal in respect of quality," said Anil Saboo, a leading oilmeal broker in the central city of Indore, the hub of India's soybean processing industry.
"The soybean crop from Argentina will also provide competition," the analyst said.
Exporters said they had contracted to export 2.2 million tonnes of soymeal so far in the 1996/97 season compared with about 1.9 million tonnes at the same time a year earlier.
"The export demand is there in spite of high Indian prices because global prices are also ruling high," said another exporter.
Traders said soymeal for export was currently quoted at $300-305 per tonne FAS (free alongside ship) compared to about $220 at this time a year earlier. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
